items.q: **Give some common examples of recruitment analytics.**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — common examples of recruitment analytics:**

1. **Cost per hire**
2. **Time to fill vacant positions**
3. **Onboarding efficiency**

---

**Worth adding for a fuller answer:** the three metrics measure **money, speed and quality** of the hiring process respectively — the classic trio you would want to trade off against one another. A cheap hire that takes six months to fill is not a good hire, and a fast hire who does not survive onboarding is not a hire at all.

Recruitment analytics sits inside the wider **HCM analytics** capability, whose point is to turn HR's transaction records into **decision support** — the *data → information → insight* movement that runs through the whole subject.

**The QnA's model answer:**

**Employee portal** is a **personalizable portal designed for employee communications, content management, and integration to self-service applications.**

It covers:
1. **Benefits**
2. **Maintenance of personal data**
3. **Leave application**
4. **Accessing pay slip and payroll data**
5. **Registering to a new training**

> **Employees maintain all these data and do all these transactions themselves.**

---

**The reasoning worth adding:** the person who knows your new address is **you**. Routing that change through an HR clerk adds a delay, a transcription error and a cost — and produces data that is no fresher than the day you got round to telling them. **Self-service moves data entry to the person who holds the knowledge**, which improves both cost and data quality at the same time.

Note the MCQ-bank statement: *"Employee self service is a part of personnel management"* → **TRUE**, even though the HCM wheel draws ESS as its own segment.

items.q: **List the areas covered by an ERP HCM module. Which process does the module as a whole implement?**
items.answer:
**The ten areas on the HCM wheel:**

1. **Recruitment**
2. **Personnel Management**
3. **Time, Leave, Attendance**
4. **Benefits and Payroll**
5. **Compensation Management**
6. **Talent / Performance Management**
7. **Learning Management**
8. **Workforce Scheduling**
9. **Employee Self Service**
10. **Employee Health & Safety (EHS)**

**The module as a whole implements the Hire-to-Retire (H2R) process.**

---

**Present them in life-cycle order rather than as a list** — it shows you understand why the set is what it is:

| Stage of the employee's life | Area |
|---|---|
| Before they join | **Recruitment** |
| The day they join | **Personnel Management** *(the record)* |
| Every day thereafter | **Time, Leave, Attendance** · **Workforce Scheduling** |
| Every month | **Benefits and Payroll** · **Compensation Management** |
| Every year | **Talent / Performance Management** · **Learning Management** |
| Throughout | **Employee Self Service** · **Employee Health & Safety** |

**Recruit → record → schedule → pay → develop**, with **ESS** as the channel the employee uses and **EHS** as the duty of care running underneath.

**Close with the chapter summary:** HCM *"brings in a holistic treatment of employees and is becoming key to modern enterprises for employee satisfaction and productivity"*, **makes the system more professional and objective**, and **supports maintenance of records for compliance.**

items.q: **Distinguish between strategic and operational HR processes, with examples. Why does the distinction matter for ERP?**
items.answer:
**HR processes group into two kinds:**

| **Strategic / Core** | **Operational / Routine** |
|---|---|
| Performance management process **design** | Employee records administration |
| Compensation **planning** | Leave and absence management |
| **Planning** job roles | Time and attendance |
| Recruitment process **design** | Tax and statutory administration |
| Workforce **planning** | **Payroll** |
| Learning strategy | Benefits administration |

**The reliable test:** strategic processes contain the words **"design"** or **"planning"**. Operational processes are **the running of the thing**.

> **Design it or plan it = strategic. Run it every month = operational.**

---

**Why it matters for ERP:** the operational column is almost exactly the **first wave** of HR automation — high volume, objective rules, automated first. The strategic column is the **last wave** — low volume, judgement-based.

**The two classifications are one fact:** the processes ERP automates first are precisely the operational ones, **because being rule-governed is what makes something both *operational* and *automatable*.** A system can *record* a performance rating and *route* it for approval, but it cannot *form* the opinion.

**The three exam traps:** *planning job roles is strategic* (**TRUE**) · *payroll is strategic* (**FALSE** — operational) · *succession planning is part of learning management* (**FALSE** — it is talent management).

**One apparent oddity to pre-empt:** *learning management* appears in the strategic column though *training administration* is routine — the distinction is between **designing the learning strategy** and **booking people onto courses**.

items.q: **What are the four broad categories of applications under the financial module?**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — the four broad categories are:**

1. **Financial Accounting**
2. **Management Accounting**
3. **Financial SCM**
4. **Treasury Applications**

---

**Expand each by the question it answers and the audience it serves** — that is what turns a four-item list into a full-mark answer:

| Category | The question it answers | Audience |
|---|---|---|
| **Financial Accounting** | *What happened?* — the statutory record | **outside** — regulators, shareholders, auditors |
| **Management Accounting** | *Where did the money go, and was it worth it?* | **inside** — managers |
| **Financial SCM** | *Will the customer actually pay us?* | **customers** |
| **Treasury** | *Do we have cash, and what is it doing?* | **banks and markets** |

The first two are the classic accounting split — **external vs internal reporting**. Financial accounting is **legally mandated and format-constrained**; management accounting is **discretionary and shaped to whatever the business needs to decide.** FSCM and Treasury both look **outward with money**: one at money coming in from customers, one at money held with banks.

*(In SAP terms this is the **FI-CO** pairing — Financial Accounting and Controlling.)*

items.q: **What are the different areas under financial accounting?**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — areas under financial accounting:**

1. **Accounts Payable**
2. **Automates and streamlines the Invoice-to-Payment cycle**
3. **Accounts Receivable / Collection Management**
4. **Payment receipt process from customer**
5. **Credit checks, risk management, customer service**
6. **Accounting GL — trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports**

*(Items 2 and 4–5 are elaborations of AP and AR respectively — quote them, they carry marks.)*

---

**Structure it as three areas with their content:**

| Area | What it covers | Cycle it closes |
|---|---|---|
| **Accounts Payable** | automates and streamlines the **Invoice-to-Payment cycle** | **Procure-to-Pay** |
| **Accounts Receivable / Collection Management** | **payment receipt from customer**; **credit checks, risk management, customer service** | **Order-to-Cash** |
| **General Ledger** | **trial balance, balance sheets, audit reports** | everything posts here |

**Direction check:** *Accounts **P**ayable = we **P**ay; Accounts **R**eceivable = we **R**eceive.*

**The GL deserves a closing line:** it is **the single point where the whole enterprise's activity is visible in one place** — which is exactly why Nestlé's **nine different general ledgers** were so damaging, and why Finance is almost always in the first implementation wave.

items.q: **Explain the five levels of ERP MRP II.**
items.answer:
**The QnA's model answer — the five levels, with the purpose of each:**

**1. Business Plan**
> **Purpose:** This plan talks about **long-term goals, objectives, business direction** in terms of **product lines, markets** etc., and is **jointly agreed by all teams in the organization** — i.e. **Marketing, Production, Finance and Engineering.**

**2. Sales and Operations Plan (S&OP)**
> **Purpose:** This is a **joint plan developed by the Sales and Marketing team together.** It details **the quantities of different product groups** that need to be produced in each period (i.e. every week or month), and the **resources (machine capacity, labor, materials etc.) needed for each period**, and does a **capacity availability check through Resource Planning.**

**3. Master Production Scheduling (MPS)**
> **Purpose:** This plan details the **plan of finished products to be made in each period** (typically every week). Against this plan an **availability check is done through Rough Cut Capacity Planning.** This plan is **also used for Available-to-Promise check and to promise the date of delivery to the customer.**

**4. Materials Requirement Planning (MRP)**
> **Purpose:** This is a **plan for production and purchase of components** needed for making the items in the master production schedule. It tells **how much quantity is needed** (based on the finished goods **Bill of Material**) and **when it is needed** (based on **manufacturing and supplier's lead time**).

**5. Purchasing and Production Activity Control**
> **Purpose:** This is the **implementation phase** of production planning and control systems. While **purchasing controls the flow of materials from vendor to factory**, **production activity control plans and controls the flow of work through the factory.**

---

**Mnemonic to reproduce the order: "Business Says Make More Products"** — **B**usiness Plan → **S**&OP → **M**PS → **M**RP → **P**AC.

**Two structural points worth stating explicitly:**

- **Each level is more detailed and shorter-horizon than the one above it.** S&OP plans **product groups**; MPS plans **finished products**; MRP plans **components**. The unit of planning gets finer as you descend.
- **Each planning level has a matching capacity check** — **S&OP ↔ RP**, **MPS ↔ RCCP**, **MRP ↔ CRP**, **PAC ↔ CC** — and level 5 is where **planning becomes execution.**

items.q: **Explain the Level and Chase strategies in Sales and Operations Planning. Which would you use, and why?**
items.answer:
**The two strategies absorb the same demand variation in two different places:**

| | **Level strategy** | **Chase strategy** |
|---|---|---|
| Production rate | **held constant** across periods | **varies to follow demand** |
| Variation absorbed in | **inventory** | **capacity** |
| Cost paid | **holding stock** — storage, obsolescence, tied-up cash | **overtime, hiring and firing, subcontracting** |
| Suits | stable products, cheap storage, expensive capacity change | perishable or bulky products, flexible workforce |

**Level** builds ahead in slow periods and draws down in busy ones. **Chase** matches output to demand period by period.

---

**The underlying reason both exist:** **capacity is fixed in the short run** — you cannot buy half a machine or hire a skilled operator for one afternoon — while **demand varies continuously.** Two quantities that move differently **cannot match by themselves**, so the mismatch must be bought somewhere. Level buys it as **stock**; Chase buys it as **flexible capacity**.

**In practice a hybrid is normal** — hold a level base load and chase the peaks — because the pure strategies each fail at one extreme.

**Note the same trade-off recurs twice more in this unit:** in **capacity planning** *(overtime, outsourcing, subcontracting to create extra capacity)*, and in **DRP** *(stock held centrally is more efficient; stock held locally is more responsive)*.

items.q: **What is Available-to-Promise (ATP), and why does it sit at the MPS level?**
items.answer:
**ATP is the check that answers a customer's question — *"can you deliver by this date?"* — from the plan rather than from stock alone.**

The QnA states it as part of MPS's purpose: *"This plan is also used for **Available-to-Promise check** and to **promise the date of delivery to the customer**."*

**Why it belongs at MPS specifically:**

- MPS is the level that plans **finished products** — and a customer buys a **finished product**, not a component. There is no other level whose unit of planning matches what is being promised.
- MPS is **capacity-checked by RCCP**, so what it holds is not merely a wish list; a promise made against it has already survived a reality check.
- It is **near enough in to be concrete** but **far enough out to still be changeable** — the horizon where a delivery commitment is meaningful.

**The deeper point:** ATP is what lets a company promise **against future planned production**, not just against **stock on hand**. Without it, sales can only sell what is physically in the warehouse; with it, they can sell what will exist — which is the entire commercial value of having a production plan at all.

**Connect it to time fences:** the reliability of an ATP promise depends on which zone the date falls in — **frozen (no change) near in, open (± 20%) far out.**

items.q: **What is a Bill of Material? Explain BOM explosion with the concept of low-level code.**
items.answer:
**Bill of Material:**
- **Also called the Product Structure**
- **The most important master data for MRP and product costing**
- **Defines which raw materials / components are needed to make an end product, and the required quantity of children for each parent**
- **BOMs can have multiple levels and can be very complex**
- **Types: CADBOM · EBOM (Engineering BOM) · MBOM (Manufacturing BOM)**

> *"In a sense, **BOM is like a recipe for a dish**!"*

**BOM explosion:** *"any MRP run does a BOM explosion — i.e. **break up the end product (parent) sequentially into its lower-level components (children) down to fundamental components**."*

---

**Low-level code** — *"MRP always happens in a sequence… this sequence of planning is driven by something known as the **low-level code**."*

**The deck's worked example** *(A is the end product)*:

| Item | Low level code |
|---|---|
| **A** | **0** |
| **B** | **1** |
| **C** | **1, 3** → **3** |
| **D** | **2** |
| **E** | **3** |

**C appears at both level 1 and level 3, so its low-level code is 3 — the lowest (deepest) level at which it occurs.**

**Why it must be the deepest occurrence** *(this is the part that earns the marks)*: C is used directly in **A** (level 1) *and* inside **D** (level 3). If MRP planned C when it first met it at level 1, it would compute C's requirement **from A alone** — and then later discover that **D also needs C**, after C's order had already been placed.

> **The rule is: plan an item only once, and only after all its demand is known.**

This is the same logic as **topological ordering** — you cannot compute a node until all its predecessors are done.

**Finish on the BOM types**, which are not three versions of one list but the same product seen by three functions: **EBOM** as the *designers* structure it (by function); **MBOM** as the *factory* needs it (by assembly sequence, including packaging and consumables the engineer never lists). **EBOM ≠ MBOM**, and reconciling them is a real problem in practice.

items.q: **An order is received for 25 units of item A. Quantities on hand are A = 3, B = 7, C = 16, D = 4, E = 6. Compute the gross and net requirements at each level, and explain the two mechanisms your calculation demonstrates.**
items.answer:
$$\textbf{Net requirement} = \textbf{Gross requirement} - \textbf{Quantity on hand}$$

| Step | Item | Gross requirement | On hand | **Net requirement** |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | **A** | 25 | 3 | **22** |
| 1 | **B** *(1 per A)* | 22 | 7 | **15** |
| 2 | **D** *(1 per B)* | 15 | 4 | **11** |
| 3 | **C** *(1 per A and D)* | **22 + 11 = 33** | 16 | **17** |
| 4 | **E** *(1 per D)* | 11 | 6 | **5** |

---

**Mechanism 1 — the net requirement at one level becomes the gross requirement at the next.**

A's net is **22**, so B's gross is **22**. B's net is **15**, so D's gross is **15**. This is precisely what the MCQ means by *"the BOM contains information necessary to **convert (explode) net requirements at one level into gross requirements at the next level**."*

**Mechanism 2 — item C is why low-level code exists.**

C is used *1 per A* **and** *1 per D*, so its gross requirement is the **sum of demand from both parents**:

$$\underbrace{22}_{\text{from A}} + \underbrace{11}_{\text{from D}} = 33$$

Had C been planned at level 1, its gross would have been **22** and the **11 from D would have been missed**. Because C carries **low-level code 3**, it is planned only after D's net requirement is known — and both demands are captured.

**State the order of operations explicitly:** explosion produces the **gross** requirement; subtracting stock produces the **net**. ⚠️ *"Exploding the BOM"* and *"netting"* are **two different steps**, and the MCQ bank tests exactly that confusion.

items.q: **Write short notes on any four MRP fundamentals: planning horizon, lot sizing, backward scheduling, time fences, exception messages.**
items.answer:
**The eight fundamentals are:** planning horizon · planning sequence and low-level code · dependency related · gross & net requirement calculations · **lot sizing procedures** · **backward scheduling** · **time fences** · **exception messages.**

---

**1. Planning horizon** — *"the period for which the planning is done."* If the horizon is one month, only **that month's demand elements** are considered. **This necessitates the planning run to happen on a regular basis** — monthly, in that case.

> The horizon creates an obligation: **because you only plan a window, you must re-plan when the window moves.** This is the *rolling* nature of MRP, and it is why **"timely and accurate replanning"** is named as MRP's major strength.

**2. Lot sizing** —

| Type | Procedures |
|---|---|
| **Static** *(fix the quantity)* | lot-for-lot · replenish to maximum stock level · fixed lot size |
| **Periodic** *(fix the interval)* | daily · weekly · monthly · planning calendar |

> *"Lot sizing is primarily for **optimizing** — transportation / packing costs and other overheads."* Ordering exactly what you need *is* lot-for-lot and minimises inventory, but **every order carries a fixed cost regardless of size**. **Lot sizing trades ordering cost against holding cost.**

**3. Backward scheduling** — used when delivery dates are known or committed:

$$\textbf{Purchase requisition date} = \textbf{MRP date} - \textbf{GR processing time} - \textbf{Vendor lead time} - \textbf{Purchasing processing time}$$

> **Three delays, three subtractions.** The most-forgotten is the first — material at the gate is **not yet usable**; it must be received, inspected and put away. *"Backward planning is almost always there whenever there is a **constraint-based delivery**."*

**4. Time fences** —

| Zone | To due date | Change allowed |
|---|---|---|
| **Frozen** | 1–2 weeks | **none** |
| **Firm** | 2–4 weeks | **± 5%** |
| **Full** | 4–6 weeks | **± 10%** |
| **Open** | 6+ weeks | **± 20%** |

> **The logic is commitment.** Material within two weeks is already ordered and possibly on the machine. **Time fences reconcile manufacturing's need for a stable schedule with sales' need for flexibility** — stability near in, flexibility far out.

**5. Exception messages** — *values outside the expected range or impossible; below safety stock; needs to be corrected and re-run; prioritize the messages → take action.*

> An MRP run over thousands of items produces thousands of planned orders. **Exception messages are how the system directs human attention.**

items.q: **What are the limitations of MRP? Explain closed-loop MRP as the response to the central one.**
items.answer:
**MRP's seven stated limitations:**

1. **It only projects how much material or capacity is required to meet the sales forecast**
2. **Cannot consider actual capacity available on the shop floor, constraints and vendor's limitations, and plan accordingly**
3. **Cannot do any optimization**
4. **Requires very high accuracy of data** — BOM data, system stock etc.
5. **Cannot replan fast enough**
6. **Requires high user discipline**
7. **Not appropriate for all areas** like **project or engineer-to-order manufacturing**, as **every new order has a unique Bill of Material**

**Group them to show structure:** ① ② are **what it cannot see**; ③ ⑤ are **what it cannot do**; ④ ⑥ are **what it demands of you**; ⑦ is **where it does not fit**.

> **④ and ⑥ are the ones that bite in practice** — *"Garbage In, Garbage Out"* landing in production planning. **An MRP run on a wrong BOM confidently orders the wrong parts.**

---

**Closed-loop MRP — the response to limitation ②:**

**MRP is known as an infinite planning tool** — *it does not consider available capacity while planning (**assumes capacity is infinite**)*. Consequently:

- **MRP can give production or procurement plans which are not executable**, as the factory or supplier capacity needed **is not available**
- **So it is important to do a reality check of the plan**
- **If the plan is not executable, the production plan for finished goods must be changed at the MPS stage, and a fresh MRP run is needed**
- **Thus MRP is a process of iterative planning — that is why it is also known as closed-loop MRP**

$$\textbf{S\&OP} \rightarrow \textbf{MPS} \rightarrow \textbf{MRP} \rightarrow \textbf{CRP} \rightarrow \textbf{Realistic?}$$
**No** → feedback to **MPS**, re-run · **Yes** → execute **production, material and capacity plans**

**The mechanism, stated plainly:** MRP works **backwards from the schedule** through the BOM and lead times. That arithmetic is perfectly correct and says **nothing about whether the factory can do the work** — it will happily produce a plan requiring 300 machine-hours in a week from a plant with 120.

⚠️ **Note where the correction is applied — at MPS, not at MRP.** If capacity cannot support the plan, you build **fewer finished products**, which changes what sales can promise. **The constraint propagates upward.**

**Balance the answer with the deck's own caveat:** *"many of the limitations are drawbacks **in comparison to other products**; in some cases **there may not be better alternatives**. One can say these are **pointers for improvement**."*

items.q: **Explain capacity planning: the balancing problem, the four levels, and how ERP supports it.**
items.answer:
**The balancing problem:**

- **A** — at any time, organizations have **"defined" resources / limited capacity**: plants, machines, people, raw material stock
- **B** — **customer needs might fluctuate up/down** in type, quantity and timelines
- **A is not directly linked to B**, hence a mismatch results in **under-utilization** or **overload / insufficient capacity**
- **Capacity planning is to balance A and B**, using strategies like **overtime, outsourcing, sub-contracting to create extra capacity**

> *"Knowing the exact capacity required of everything needed is **non-trivial**."*

**Why the mismatch is structural, not a planning failure:** capacity is **fixed in the short run** — you cannot buy half a machine or hire a skilled operator for one afternoon — while demand is **continuously variable**. So the mismatch always shows up as one of two costs: **idle capacity you are paying for**, or **demand you cannot serve**. The listed strategies are all ways of **buying short-term capacity at a premium** rather than owning it year-round.

---

**The four levels — MRP II suggests capacity planning at each planning level:**

| Capacity technique | Planning level it checks |
|---|---|
| **Resource Planning (RP)** | **S&OP** |
| **Rough Cut Capacity Planning (RCCP)** | **MPS** |
| **Capacity Requirement Planning (CRP)** | **MRP** |
| **Capacity Control (CC)** | **PAC** — shop-floor detailed scheduling |

**The checks get finer as you descend, exactly like the plans they check.** RP asks a rough question about whole plants over months; CC manages actual machine loading on a shift. **"Rough Cut" is named honestly** — at MPS level you check only the **critical resources**, because the plan is not detailed enough to justify more.

**The deck's note on the gaps:** *"there will be **gaps between each planning level and also with execution levels**… plans need to be **tracked at each level and kept refining at lower levels**, adjusting to deviations from preceding steps."*

---

**ERP support for capacity management:**
- **Capacity evaluation at each resource level**
- **Scheduling of orders based on capacity**
- **Allow processing of orders in parts to match capacity**
- **Schedule with forward planning feature**

⚠️ **But: "most of these are semi-automated and need 'manual' actions"**, and **"ERP's support for capacity management is a little indirect."** ERP **evaluates** capacity and **presents** the conflict; the resolution — overtime, subcontract, re-sequence — is largely a **human decision made outside the system.** *"Specialized supply chain apps with **APS — Advanced Planning and Scheduling** — have a much better capability here."*

**Worth adding:** capacity planning is *"a **higher-order managerial task**… **in services business, capacity planning is quite crucial since this dictates cost estimations and hence quote pricing** — so this is also a **competitive parameter**."*

items.q: **What are the critical master data elements for production planning? Describe each.**
items.answer:
**Four types of master data** — *"a key piece of ERP is maintaining the master data elements required for production"*:

**Mnemonic — "My BOM Works Right"**, and each answers a different question:

| Element | Question |
|---|---|
| **Material Master** | **what** is it? |
| **Bill of Material** | **what goes into** it? |
| **Work Center** | **where** is it made? |
| **Routing** | **in what order** is it made? |

---

**1. Material Master** — *lots of information related to material: identification, cost, measures, planning parameters*, **generally represented as views, similar to "database views"**. *"It is sufficiently complicated that **expertise in just SAP MM is a job profile by itself!**"*

**Its four data segments:**

| Segment | Examples |
|---|---|
| **General Data** | material number, description, units of measure, weight, volume, product hierarchy |
| **Plant Specific** | MRP profile, production costs, planning data, valuation |
| **Storage Location Specific** | quantities, special stock, warehouse attributes |
| **Sales Specific** | delivering plant, sales text, sales units, shipping data, division |

> **Why the segmentation exists:** the same material means different things in different places. Weight is the same everywhere; the MRP profile may differ between plants; stock differs by location; the sales unit may differ by channel. So the record is **one general core plus per-plant, per-location and per-sales-org extensions** — which lets a company hold **one material number** enterprise-wide while recording local differences.

**Views** include: **Basic · Purchasing · MRP · Work scheduling · Forecast · Sales · Costing · Accounting · Quality Management · Warehouse Management · Classification · Plant/Storage location stocks.** The deck's point about them is about **access**, not convenience: *"a **purchase clerk might have access to 'sensitive' information such as cost price, but the works manager may not** — even though in the org structure he is 'superior'."* **Access follows the job, not the rank.**

**2. Bill of Material** — the product structure; **"the most important master data for MRP and product costing."**

**3. Work Centers** — **machine / people / production line where the activity is performed**; **closely linked to the "cost center" of the finance module**; **key element to determine scheduling, capacity planning and costing.**

> **The work centre ↔ cost centre link is the integration point between production and finance.** The work centre is where work physically happens; the cost centre is where cost is recorded. Without that link, manufacturing knows how long things took and finance knows what things cost, and **nobody can connect the two.**

**4. Routing** — **operation sequence to produce finished goods**; **material moves from one work center to the next at successive levels of job completion**; **important for scheduling.** *"Combination of work center and routing provides ample scope for **optimizing combinations**."*

**The worked example:**

| Operation | Time | Work Center | Function | Cost Center |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **10** | **20 min** | **W1** | Assembly | **100** |
| **20** | **15 min** | **W2** | Painting | **200** |
| **30** | **10 min** | **W3** | Finishing | **300** |

This one table does **three jobs at once** — **sequencing** *(10, 20, 30 — stepping by ten so an operation can be inserted without renumbering)*, **scheduling** *(45 minutes of work content per unit)*, and **costing** *(each work centre linked to a cost centre)*.

$$\textbf{Routing} \times \textbf{quantity} \rightarrow \textbf{load per work centre} \rightarrow \textbf{capacity check} + \textbf{cost}$$

**This is where CRP gets its numbers from.**

items.q: **Describe the different production scenarios and the specific ERP requirements of each.**
items.answer:
| Scenario | Characteristics | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| **Process Industry** | **Batch management, recipe, PI sheets, interface of ERP with PLC / process automation equipment** | **chemical, oil and gas, pharmaceutical, petrochemical** |
| **Repetitive Manufacturing** | **Product less complex, more stable, long periods of the same product; material staging, back flushing** | **consumer goods (FMCG), electronics** |
| **Kanban / Just In Time (JIT)** | **JIT, Kanban** | industries using Kanban or JIT |

**Scenario-specific requirements:**

**For Process Industry** — **Batch Management** *(chemical properties may differ; for tracking)* · **Characteristics** *(different parameters to define different materials)* · **Recipe ⟺ BOM in process industry** · **Process Instruction Sheet** for the process operator

**For Repetitive Manufacturing** — **period and quantity based production plan** · **back flushing** *(shift/day's finished goods produced and BOM consumed quantities for batch update and inventory reduction)* · **specialized material staging near the assembly line**

**For Kanban / JIT** — **electronic Kanban card** *(material, quantity, destination details)* · **triggers delivery from demand source to supply source** · **Kanban quantity calculation** to store beside the operator

---

**Why the three differ at all:** they sit on a spectrum of **how discrete the product is.** Process industry makes things you **measure** — litres, tonnes — and two batches genuinely differ. Repetitive makes identical discrete units **continuously**. Kanban makes discrete units too, but **pulled by consumption** rather than pushed by a schedule.

**This is also the deepest reason ERP requires configuration:** *"this is the place where a lot of **'customization' is needed based on type of industry**."*

**Two concepts worth expanding if marks allow:**

- **Back flushing inverts the normal flow** — instead of issuing materials then producing, you **record the finished goods and work backwards through the BOM** to deduct what must have been consumed. It suits repetitive manufacturing because the BOM is reliable there. ⚠️ **Its cost: scrap, rework and substitutions are invisible to it**, so inventory drifts and must be corrected by physical counts. **It buys speed with accuracy.**
- **Kanban is a pull system** — the card *"triggers delivery from demand source to supply source"*, i.e. **the demand end initiates**. **Toyota** conceived the term; it means **"visual sign" or "visual card"**, and in the **1940s** the cards were **paper notes on a physical board**, used *"to create a transparent work process and reduce production waste."*

items.q: **What is Distribution Requirement Planning? State its objectives, inputs and outputs, and explain how it relates to MRP.**
items.answer:
**Definition:**
- **DRP is the process of shipment of finished goods from manufacturing locations to end customers**
- **It is a network of warehouses, distribution centers and wholesalers / retailers**
- **DRP is not part of the MRP II flow, but it is an extension of MRP logic of manufacturing to the distribution network**
- **Provides a time-based finished goods inventory replenishment plan in the distribution network**
- **DRP translates local distribution center requirements into central distribution center requirements, then into central warehouse requirements, and finally into gross requirements at the factory**

$$\textbf{LDC} \rightarrow \textbf{CDC} \rightarrow \textbf{CWH} \rightarrow \textbf{Factory}$$

**The distribution network:** **Factory → Central distribution facility → Regional centre → Local warehouse → Retailer**

**Objectives:**
1. **Improve customer service levels** by **anticipating customer demand at distribution centers** and **providing finished products at the correct location**
2. **Provide an accurate requirements plan for manufacturing** — matching material supply to manufacturing demand, and customer demand to product supply
3. **Optimize the distribution of available stock in the network**
4. **Minimize finished goods inbound inventory in the network**

**Inputs:** **forecast of demand for each SKU** (gross requirement) · **current inventory level of the SKU** (balance on hand) · **target safety stock** · **lead time for replenishment** · **in transit** (scheduled receipts) · **planned shipments / planned order releases**

**Outputs:** **stock transport requisitions between locations** — *which goods, of what quantity, to where and when* — **between any of factory, warehouse, distribution center.**

---

**How it relates to MRP — this is the analytical part of the answer.** The DRP inputs are the MRP inputs **with the network substituted for the BOM**:

| MRP | DRP |
|---|---|
| MPS — what to build | **forecast of demand per SKU** |
| BOM — what goes into it | **the distribution network** |
| Inventory status | **inventory + in transit + safety stock** |
| Lead times | **replenishment lead time** |
| → purchase requisitions / planned orders | → **stock transport requisitions** |

**DRP explodes a network the way MRP explodes a BOM**, and the worked DRP plan shows the same netting arithmetic per location, week by week — *Period Usage, Gross Requirement, Beginning Inventory, Scheduled Receipts, Net Requirement, Planned Receipt, Ending Inventory, Planned Order* — for a **Central Warehouse (Q=200, SS=0, LT=2)** and a **Regional Warehouse (Q=50, SS=15, LT=1)**.

⚠️ **Note the direction:** requirements flow **inward from the customer end toward the factory**, not outward.

**A good closing observation:** **objectives 1 and 4 are in tension.** *Providing products at the correct location* wants stock **close to the customer**; *minimizing network inventory* wants it **concentrated centrally**. **Stock held centrally is more efficient; stock held locally is more responsive** — and DRP is the calculation that decides where the line falls.

*(DRP is **one of the core areas that evolved into SCP — Supply Chain Planning**.)*

items.q: **Trace the evolution of ERP from MRP to ERP II. How do the niche enterprise applications relate to it?**
items.answer:
| Period | ERP Outlook |
|---|---|
| **1960–70s** | **MRP — Material Requirement Planning.** Inventory and process time reduction with new production planning systems |
| **1980s** | **MRP II — Manufacturing Resource Planning.** Greater reduction due to **integration with accounting, billing** |
| **1990s** | **ERP.** **All processes integrated**; collaboration with other enterprise apps like CRM, SRM; **supports non-manufacturing too** |
| **2000s** | **Extended ERP, ERP II.** **Focussed on clients, optimizing the whole business network — including suppliers and clients** |

**The pattern — each decade adds one ring outward:**

$$\textbf{Materials} \rightarrow \textbf{the Factory} \rightarrow \textbf{the Enterprise} \rightarrow \textbf{the Network}$$

| Decade | Scope | One-word test |
|---|---|---|
| **1960–70s** | materials | can I get the **parts**? |
| **1980s** | the whole plant, plus accounting and billing | can the **factory** do it, and at what cost? |
| **1990s** | the whole company, manufacturing or not | is the **enterprise** integrated? |
| **2000s** | suppliers and customers too | is the **network** optimised? |

**Each expansion is the previous one's limitation resolved.** MRP could not see capacity — MRP II added it. MRP II only served factories — ERP served everyone. ERP stopped at the company wall — ERP II crossed it.

**The deck's own expansions:**
- **MRP** — *"uses the master production schedules — what needs to be manufactured, how much, how much in stock, how much to order. **First application of computing to the manufacturing process.** Closed loop — little simplistic, does not consider constraints of capacity."*
- **MRP II** — *"**not just production**, but considers other functions such as capacity, financial, HR, supply chain, billing."*
- **ERP** — *"all that is MRP and MRP II + other things such as HR, collaborate with other enterprise apps… **e-Business applications started coming.**"*

⚠️ **"Supports non-manufacturing too" is precisely the moment the word "Manufacturing" left the name** — *Manufacturing* Resource Planning became *Enterprise* Resource Planning because the customers were no longer only factories.

---

**The niche applications:**
- **ERP functionalities have evolved over time; so also the non-integrated niche enterprise "functional" applications such as CRM, SRM**
- **Lots of overlap in functionality**
- **They may co-exist within an enterprise**

The *earlier vs now* tables show every one of them making the same move — **transaction → decision**: SCM went from *recording where stock is* to **demand planning and optimization**; SRM from *paying the vendor* to **auctions and supplier analytics**; CRM from *invoicing* to **opportunity management**. **Every "earlier" entry is a transaction that already happened; every "now" entry is a decision about what should happen.**

**The sharpest evidence of overlap:** **EAM and SRM have word-for-word identical "earlier" columns** — *Procurement · Vendor payment · Vendor rating.* Two separate product categories once did the very same thing.

**Why the overlap never closes:** *"**ERP functionalities are getting comprehensive to include the niche functionalities at each newer version, but the specialized products are getting specialized further and maintain independent identity.**"* **Both sides are running.**

**Hence the real decision, in the deck's words:** *"A company has to carefully weigh whether to go for an **enterprise app that is critical to its business**, or go for an **integrated ERP**. Even in ERP, **modules can be separately implemented**. **It is not an easy decision.**"* — the **best-of-breed vs single-vendor** trade-off from package selection.
